Motion rules
  • All motion uses one gentle curve, (0.25, 0.8, 0.25, 1), with no bounce, about 20% quicker than v9.
  • Push: next screen slides in, the last one drifts 15% behind and dims. 520 ms.
  • Sheet: rises from the bottom, 560 ms; closes in 360 ms. Drag down to close.
  • Nearby list: follows your finger, opens or settles in 480 ms.
  • Swipe pages follow your finger and settle in 520 ms. Edges stretch at 30%.
  • Tutorial highlight glides to the next control, 520 ms.
  • Map modes, tabs and Summary/Detailed: crossfade, 360 ms.
  • Press: scale 0.98, 180 ms. Banner: fades down 12 px, 420 ms, stays 2.6 s.
  • Stamp: fades in from 1.08×, 650 ms.
  • Year rail: the chip follows the text as you scroll; the year fades in over 240 ms when it changes.
  • Reduce motion: every change becomes a 150 ms fade, and loops stop.

Story text drafted with AI from published biographies of Yun Dong-ju; check facts before testing. Photos: Korea Heritage Service (국가유산청), heritage.go.kr. They carry no KOGL mark, so ask the agency before public use. Maps and walking distances: Mapbox (© Mapbox © OpenStreetMap). v12 (18 Nov): Era button on the map (Now · 1942 · 1927 · 1861 · 1420s Sejong) using Seoul Historical Archive maps; contour terrain map; Korean language (EN/한 button); Field notes beta (photo + short note, kept on this device only); third tab; class-demo note on the first screen. v11: the three map screens are one map you can drag and zoom around Sinchon (Yonsei, Ewha, Sinchon station, Nogosan), with 13 pins; tap a pin for its archive photos and a walking route. Map images: Mapbox light and outdoors styles, saved with the page; distances and routes from Mapbox walking directions. Archive photos: Seoul Museum of History, Seoul Historical Archive (서울역사아카이브), KOGL Type 1 (free to use with credit); check each record page before public use. Pins marked approximate need checking on site. Places and dates from the heritage portal; the Main Gate year is the June 1987 event (Lee Han-yeol), not a building date.

No. 02 · Pinson Hall, Yonsei

Yun Dong-ju Poetry Stone

윤동주 시비

Yun Dong-ju came to Yonhi College, the school that later became Yonsei, in 1938. He lived here, in the dormitory now called Pinson Hall, and wrote many of his best-known poems while he studied.

Korea was under Japanese colonial rule. The Korean language was being pushed out of schools and newspapers, but Yun kept writing in Korean: quiet poems about the sky, the wind and the stars, and about the shame of not doing more.

Look here Pinson Hall

Look at the slope in front of the building: the poem stone stands there. It is carved with "Prologue", which he wrote in November 1941.

In 1942 he went to study in Japan. A year later he was arrested for "independence activity" and sent to Fukuoka prison. He died there in February 1945, aged 27, six months before Korea was freed.

Before he left, he had copied out his poems by hand. A friend's mother hid one copy under the floorboards of her house. The poems were published in 1948, and this stone was put up in 1968.

Growing up outside Korea

Yun Dong-ju was born in 1917 in Myeongdong, a Korean village in Jiandao, in what is now northeast China. Many Korean families had settled there, and the village had its own church and school. His cousin Song Mong-gyu was born in the same house a few months earlier, and the two grew up and studied side by side.

Four years at Yonhi

In 1938 both cousins entered the literature department of Yonhi College. Yun lived in the college dormitory behind this slope, now called Pinson Hall, a Gothic building faced with dark-brown stone quarried from nearby Ansan. Most of the poems he is remembered for were written in these years.

Korea had been ruled by Japan since 1910. By the late 1930s, under Japanese colonial rule, Korean was being removed from school lessons, Korean newspapers were being shut down, and people were pressed to take Japanese names. Writing in Korean was becoming risky.

The book that was never printed

In 1941, as he was about to graduate, Yun chose nineteen poems for a first collection and called it Sky, Wind, Stars and Poems. Printing it seemed too dangerous, and his teacher advised him to wait. Instead he made three copies by hand: one for himself, one for his teacher Lee Yang-ha, and one for his younger friend Jeong Byeong-uk.

Look here Pinson Hall

Look at the slope in front of the building, now the Yun Dong-ju Memorial Hall: the poem stone stands there. It is carved with "Prologue", the poem that opens the collection, dated 20 November 1941. It begins:

Until the day I die, looking up at the sky, I hope to have not a speck of shame."Prologue", 1941 · our translation

Japan

In 1942 he left to study in Japan, first at Rikkyo University in Tokyo and then at Doshisha University in Kyoto. To get his travel papers he had to register a Japanese name. Days before he did, he wrote a poem called "Confession".

In July 1943 he and Song Mong-gyu were arrested by the Kyoto police for "independence activity". Yun was sentenced to two years and sent to Fukuoka prison. He died there on 16 February 1945, at 27. Song died in the same prison a few weeks later. Korea was freed that August.

Hidden under the floor

Jeong Byeong-uk was drafted into the Japanese army as a student soldier. Before he left, he gave his copy of the poems to his mother in Gwangyang, in the south of Korea, and asked her to keep it safe. She hid it under the wooden floor of the house.

After liberation, Jeong and Yun's friends gathered the poems they could find. Sky, Wind, Stars and Poems was finally published in January 1948, three years after Yun's death.

This stone

In 1968, students and graduates of Yonsei put up this stone in front of the dormitory where he had lived. Today Yun Dong-ju is one of the most widely read poets in Korea, and "Prologue" is a poem many Koreans know by heart.

End of the story

Term

Yonhi College

연희전문학교

The old name of Yonsei University. It was founded in 1915 by the American missionary Horace G. Underwood, called Yonhi College from 1917, and joined Severance Medical College to become Yonsei in 1957.

Term

Japanese colonial rule

일제강점기

Japan ruled Korea from 1910 to 1945. In the later years, schools were made to teach in Japanese and Korean was pushed out of public life.
